content: 1. Waste Management in Healthcare Settings: Liquid waste, such as urine or solid fecal matter, can be safely disposed of into the sewage system if an adequate system is in place. 2. Handling and Transport of Contaminated Materials: Used equipment, soiled linen, and waste from isolation areas should be placed directly into containers or bags within the isolation room. These containers or bags must be sealed securely to prevent spillage during transport. Double bagging is unnecessary if the outer surface of the bag remains uncontaminated. All personnel handling these materials must follow standard precautions and perform hand hygiene after removing PPE. 3. Prevention of Needle Stick and Sharp Injuries: Preventing injuries from needles, scalpels, and other sharp instruments is critical to reducing the transmission of bloodborne pathogens. Used needles should never be recapped, bent, or removed from syringes by hand. All sharp items must be disposed of in puncture-resistant containers located near the point of use. Reusable syringes should be avoided. 4. Droplet Precautions: Respiratory pathogens, such as influenza, SARS, and adenovirus, are transmitted via large droplets. During an influenza pandemic, droplet precautions should be implemented alongside standard precautions. This includes wearing a medical mask when within 1 meter of the patient, placing patients in single rooms or cohorting them based on diagnosis, and limiting patient movement outside their room. Patients should wear a medical mask when outside their room. 5. Contact Precautions: Pathogens like respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and parainfluenza can spread through contact, particularly via contaminated hands. Contact precautions include wearing gloves and gowns when entering a patient’s room and ensuring that equipment is either disposable or dedicated to the patient. Shared equipment must be cleaned and disinfected between uses. 6. Airborne Precautions: For airborne pathogens, such as tuberculosis or measles, HCWs should wear particulate respirators (e.g., N95 masks) when entering isolation rooms. Patients should be placed in airborne precaution rooms with appropriate ventilation. Aerosol-generating procedures should be performed in well-ventilated rooms with proper PPE. 7. Preparation of Isolation Rooms: Isolation rooms should have appropriate hand-washing facilities, signage, and minimal furniture that is easy to clean. PPE should be readily available outside the room, and waste disposal systems should be touch-free if possible. Daily cleaning and disinfection of the room are essential. 8. PPE Usage: HCWs must don PPE in the correct order (e.g., gown, mask, eye protection, gloves) before entering isolation areas and remove it carefully to avoid contamination. Hand hygiene should be performed immediately after removing gloves and other PPE. 9. Handling of Deceased Bodies: Deceased bodies should be sealed in impermeable body bags to prevent fluid leakage and transported to the mortuary as soon as possible. HCWs handling bodies must wear disposable gowns, gloves, and facial protection if splashing is anticipated. Hand hygiene must be performed after PPE removal. 10. Use of Disinfectants: Alcohol and bleach are effective disinfectants when used appropriately. Surfaces must be cleaned of organic material before applying disinfectants. Alcohol is effective against influenza viruses but should only be used on small surfaces in well-ventilated areas. Bleach is effective but can irritate mucous membranes and corrode surfaces. It should be diluted properly and used cautiously. 11. Stockpiling PPE for Epidemics: Healthcare facilities should estimate PPE needs based on assumptions such as the frequency of HCW-patient interactions and the duration of the epidemic. Medical masks should be replaced when wet, damaged, or soiled. Respirators can be reused for tuberculosis care but should be discarded after each use for other respiratory diseases. 12. Education and Training: HCWs must be educated on the safe removal, storage, and handling of potentially contaminated equipment to minimize self-contamination and self-inoculation risks. Proper training is essential for infection prevention and control.
